sub_units.name: String Class
sub_units.content: The String class in Java represents an immutable sequence of characters. Strings are objects stored in the String pool for memory optimization. Java provides a rich set of methods for string manipulation including length(), charAt(), substring(), indexOf(), replace(), toUpperCase(), toLowerCase(), trim(), split(), and compareTo(). Understanding string immutability, the difference between == and equals() for string comparison, and the String pool concept is essential for efficient Java programming.

videos.title: String Class
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering String Class in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: StringBuilder & StringBuffer
sub_units.content: StringBuilder and StringBuffer are mutable alternatives to the String class for efficient string manipulation. Unlike String, they allow in-place modifications without creating new objects, making them ideal for scenarios involving frequent concatenation or modification. StringBuffer is thread-safe (synchronized) while StringBuilder is not, making StringBuilder faster in single-threaded environments. Key methods include append(), insert(), delete(), reverse(), and replace(). Choosing the right class depends on mutability needs and thread safety requirements.

videos.title: StringBuilder & StringBuffer
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering StringBuilder & StringBuffer in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: Exception Handling
sub_units.content: Exception handling in Java is a mechanism to handle runtime errors gracefully using try, catch, and finally blocks. Exceptions are objects that represent abnormal conditions during program execution. Java has a hierarchy of exception classes rooted at Throwable, with two main branches: checked exceptions (compile-time) and unchecked exceptions (runtime). The try block contains code that might throw an exception, catch blocks handle specific exceptions, and the finally block executes regardless of whether an exception occurred.

videos.title: Exception Handling
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Exception Handling in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: throw & throws
sub_units.content: The 'throw' keyword is used to explicitly throw an exception from a method or block of code, while 'throws' is used in a method signature to declare that a method may throw specific checked exceptions. Using 'throw', developers can create and throw exception objects manually to signal error conditions. The 'throws' clause informs the caller that they must handle the declared exceptions. Understanding the difference between throw and throws is crucial for designing robust error-handling strategies in Java applications.

videos.title: throw & throws
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering throw & throws in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: Custom Exceptions
sub_units.content: Custom exceptions in Java are user-defined exception classes that extend Exception (for checked exceptions) or RuntimeException (for unchecked exceptions). They allow developers to create meaningful, application-specific error types that provide more context than built-in exceptions. Custom exceptions typically include constructors that accept error messages and optional cause parameters. Creating well-designed custom exceptions improves code clarity, makes error handling more specific, and enhances the debugging experience.

videos.title: Custom Exceptions
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Custom Exceptions in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: File Handling Basics
sub_units.content: File handling in Java involves creating, reading, writing, and deleting files using classes from the java.io package. The File class represents file and directory pathnames. FileReader and FileWriter provide character-based file operations, while FileInputStream and FileOutputStream handle byte-based operations. Key operations include checking file existence, creating new files, reading file content line by line, writing data to files, and managing file permissions. Understanding file handling is essential for data persistence in Java applications.

videos.title: File Handling Basics
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering File Handling Basics in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: BufferedReader & BufferedWriter
sub_units.content: BufferedReader and BufferedWriter are wrapper classes that add buffering capability to character-based I/O streams for improved performance. BufferedReader reads text efficiently using an internal buffer and provides the readLine() method for reading lines. BufferedWriter writes text with buffering and provides newLine() for platform-independent line separation. Using buffered streams significantly reduces the number of I/O operations by reading and writing data in larger chunks instead of character by character.

videos.title: BufferedReader & BufferedWriter
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering BufferedReader & BufferedWriter in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: Serialization & Deserialization
sub_units.content: Serialization is the process of converting a Java object into a byte stream for storage or transmission, while deserialization reconstructs the object from the byte stream. A class must implement the Serializable interface to be serializable. ObjectOutputStream and ObjectInputStream are used for writing and reading serialized objects. The transient keyword excludes specific fields from serialization. The serialVersionUID ensures version compatibility between serialized and deserialized objects across different JVM instances.

videos.title: Serialization & Deserialization
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Serialization & Deserialization in Strings, Exception Handling & File Handling.

sub_units.name: NIO Package
sub_units.content: The Java NIO (New I/O) package, introduced in Java 1.4 and enhanced in Java 7 (NIO.2), provides an alternative to traditional I/O with improved performance and scalability. Key components include Channels (for bidirectional data transfer), Buffers (for data storage), and Selectors (for multiplexed I/O). The Path and Files classes from NIO.2 offer a modern, fluent API for file operations including reading, writing, copying, moving, and walking directory trees. NIO is especially useful for high-performance and non-blocking I/O operations.
